title: Rebaptism of those baptized by heretics is not simply necessary to salvation — Cyprian, Stephen, Augustine
source_text: XXIV. Sed adversarii vim praecipue faciunt in dogmate de non iterando baptismo in iis qui ab haereticis baptizati sunt, quasi negare non possimus dogma illud ad fidem necessario pertinere, & haereticos esse qui illud negant, nec tamen etiam possimus illud ex sacra Scriptura probare. Sed certe utrum illud sit ad salutem necessarium, si nihil aliud esset, ambiguum facere posset Cyprianus Christi Martyr, qui sancti nomen post obitum in Ecclesia meruit. Etenim dubium non est illum e vivis excessisse retinentem ejus sententiae quam Ecclesia postea communiter repudiavit. Et tamen quis auderet pronunciare salute excidisse virum doctrina, pietate, constantique in Christum fide praecellentissimum? Neque difficultatem expedit quod excipere solent adversarii ea de re tempore Cypriani nihil dum ab Ecclesia fuisse definitum: Nam si, quod Pontificii volunt, Ecclesia illud dogma accepit ab Apostolica traditione, quid ad sanctionis Apostolicae authoritatem accedere potuit ex Ecclesiae decreto? Sane si necessarium non fuit ex Apostolorum authoritate, necessarium esse non potuit ex authoritate Conciliorum. Adde quod ipso vivente Cypriano sententia ejus publice damnata & reprobata fuit a Stephano Episcopo Romano, cujus ore volunt Ecclesiam loqui, & illius rescripta esse totidem oracula Christianorum fidem obligantia. Et tamen ejus judicio Cyprianus non acquievit, sed liberum sibi putavit in sententia propria permanere, & Stephani scripta refellere. Itaque, quanquam in illam eamus sententiam, quae Ecclesiae communi judicio sancita est, nempe iterandum non esse baptismum apud haereticos susceptum, eam tamen urgere nollemus, tanquam quae sit ad salutem simpliciter necessaria. Quod vero illam sequimur ac tuemur, id non facimus quod eam alicujus verbi non scripti authoritate fultam esse putemus, sed quia, si non ex Scriptura demonstrari, probabilissime tamen ex ea colligi potest, ut manifestum faciunt argumenta quae ex Scriptura sacra sedulo in hanc rem collegit Augustinus. Ac praeterea protervum & inverecundum esset sententiam ab universali Ecclesia jam receptam, nec ulla in re Scripturae contrariam rejicere, & animi quadam libidine diversam praxin sequi ab ea quae diuturno fidelium usu probata est, nihil Scripturae repugnante.
pass_a_gloss: But the adversaries chiefly press the dogma of not reiterating baptism in those who were baptized by heretics, as if we could not deny that that dogma necessarily pertains to the faith, and that those who deny it are heretics, and yet we also could not prove it from sacred Scripture. But certainly whether that is necessary to salvation, if there were nothing else, Cyprian the Martyr of Christ, who after death merited the name of a saint in the Church, could make ambiguous. For it is not doubtful that he departed from the living retaining that opinion which the Church afterward commonly repudiated. And yet who would dare pronounce that a man most excellent in doctrine, piety, and constant faith in Christ fell from salvation? Nor does that exception which the adversaries are wont to make remove the difficulty, that nothing had yet been defined by the Church on that matter in Cyprian's time: For if, as the Pontiffs will, the Church received that dogma from Apostolic tradition, what could be added to the authority of the Apostolic sanction from a decree of the Church? Surely if it was not necessary from the Apostles' authority, it could not be necessary from the authority of Councils. Add that while Cyprian himself was living his opinion was publicly condemned and reproved by Stephen the Roman Bishop, by whose mouth they will have the Church speak, and whose rescripts they will have be so many oracles binding Christians' faith. And yet Cyprian did not acquiesce in his judgment, but thought himself free to remain in his own opinion, and to refute Stephen's writings. Therefore, although we go into that opinion which is sanctioned by the Church's common judgment, namely that baptism received among heretics is not to be reiterated, yet we would not urge it as simply necessary to salvation. And that we follow and defend it, we do not because we think it propped by the authority of some unwritten word, but because, if it cannot be demonstrated from Scripture, yet it can most probably be gathered from it, as the arguments which Augustine carefully collected from sacred Scripture on this matter make plain. And besides it would be stubborn and shameless to reject an opinion already received by the universal Church and contrary to Scripture in no point, and by a certain lust of mind to follow a practice different from that which long use of the faithful has approved, Scripture nowhere opposing.
pass_b_english: Rome presses hardest the rule against rebaptizing those baptized by heretics — as if it were necessary faith we cannot deny, yet cannot prove from Scripture.
Cyprian died holding the opposite view the Church later repudiated — yet who would say that martyr fell from salvation?
Their dodge that nothing was yet defined in Cyprian's day fails: if the dogma is Apostolic tradition, a later Church decree adds nothing to Apostolic authority.
Stephen of Rome condemned Cyprian while he lived; Cyprian refused and answered him.
We share the Church's settled practice — no rebaptism of heretics' baptism — but will not urge it as simply necessary to salvation.
We hold it not by unwritten word, but because Augustine's Scripture arguments make it highly probable — and it would be shameless to reject universal practice Scripture does not oppose.

choices.english: baptism is not to be reiterated
choices.why: Settled practice he will not elevate to simple necessity.

choices.english: by authority of an unwritten word
choices.why: Denied as the ground of their assent.
